subject: Catering Craft Practice
practicalPaper: Paper 3 is an alternative-to-practical test of five short structured questions, all compulsory, in 40 minutes for 40 marks. Questions test practical kitchen and service knowledge - identifying equipment and commodities, cooking methods and procedures, table laying, menu planning and costing/portion calculations.

practicals.title: Standard and local measurements and recipe scaling
practicals.topic: Principles of cooking methods and practical demonstrations
practicals.aim: To measure ingredients accurately with standard and local measures, convert between them and scale a recipe for a larger number of portions.
apparatus: Local measures (e.g. derica, cigarette cup/congo, mudu)
safety: Wipe spills at once to prevent slips.
Keep the scale dry.
procedure: Level dry ingredients in spoons and cups with the back of a knife; read liquids at eye level on a flat surface.
Weigh one level cup of flour, sugar and rice and record the masses.
Fill a local measure (e.g. a derica) with rice, weigh it and record its mass so that it can be used in costing.
Convert spoon and cup measures to millilitres and grams using your results.
Convert oven temperatures between °C and °F.
Scale a 10-portion recipe up to 50 portions using a conversion factor.
practicals.expectedObservations: Equal volumes of different ingredients have different masses (a cup of sugar is heavier than a cup of flour). Local measures vary from seller to seller, which is why caterers weigh ingredients for consistent results.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Standard measures: 1 teaspoon = 5 ml; 1 tablespoon = 15 ml = 3 teaspoons; 1 cup = 250 ml. If 1 level cup of flour weighs about 125 g, then 375 g flour = 375/125 = 3 cups. Temperature: °F = °C x 9/5 + 32, so 180 °C = 180 x 1.8 + 32 = 356 °F (about 350 °F, gas mark 4). Scaling: conversion factor = required portions / recipe portions = 50/10 = 5; multiply every ingredient by 5.
precautions: Level measures accurately.
Use the same type of measure throughout a recipe.
Tare the scale before each weighing.
sourcesOfError: Packed versus sifted flour gives different masses.
commonMistakes: Using heaped spoonfuls.
Reading the jug from above.
Scaling only some ingredients.
examTips: Know the standard equivalents by heart.
Show the conversion factor when scaling.

practicals.title: Culinary terms in practice: classical vegetable cuts and mise en place
practicals.aim: To demonstrate mise en place and classical cuts of vegetables (julienne, brunoise, jardinière, macédoine, paysanne) to the correct sizes.
apparatus: Chopping board on a damp cloth
safety: Use the claw grip; keep fingertips tucked in.
Keep knives sharp; place on the board, never in the sink.
Stabilise the board with a damp cloth.
procedure: Mise en place: assemble all tools and ingredients, wash and peel vegetables.
Square off the carrot to form a neat block.
Julienne: cut into thin strips about 3 mm x 3 mm x 40 mm.
Brunoise: cut julienne strips across into small dice about 2-3 mm.
Jardinière: batons about 3-4 mm x 3-4 mm x 18-20 mm; macédoine: dice about 5 mm.
Paysanne: thin, even slices of rounds, triangles or squares about 1 cm across.
Weigh the usable cut vegetables and the trimmings and calculate the yield.
practicals.expectedObservations: Evenly cut vegetables cook evenly and look professional; trimmings can be used for stocks and soups.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Carrots bought: 500 g; usable cut carrot: 420 g; trimmings/peel: 80 g. Yield % = 420/500 x 100 = 84%. Wastage % = 80/500 x 100 = 16%.
precautions: Cut uniformly.
Keep cut potatoes under water to stop browning.
Use trimmings for stock to reduce waste.
sourcesOfError: Uneven pieces make size checks inaccurate.
commonMistakes: Confusing julienne (strips) with brunoise (dice).
Rocking the knife without the claw grip.
examTips: Define culinary terms precisely and give an example dish for each.
Sizes of cuts are frequently asked.

practicals.title: Preparing white stock and a roux-based (béchamel) sauce
practicals.topic: Study of food commodities and principles of cooking methods
practicals.aim: To prepare a white chicken stock by simmering and a béchamel sauce using a white roux, and calculate yields and portions.
safety: Lift the heavy stock pot with help; strain away from the body.
Cool stock quickly and refrigerate within 2 hours.
procedure: Stock: blanch and rinse 1 kg chicken bones, cover with 3 litres of cold water and bring to the boil.
Skim, add the mirepoix and herbs, and simmer gently (do not boil) for about 2 hours, skimming regularly.
Strain, measure the yield, cool rapidly and refrigerate.
Béchamel: melt 50 g fat, stir in 50 g flour and cook gently for 2-3 minutes without colouring (white roux).
Gradually add 500 ml warm milk, stirring or whisking to keep smooth; bring to the boil and simmer for 10 minutes.
Season, strain if needed, and cover with a film of butter or paper to prevent a skin.
practicals.expectedObservations: Simmered and skimmed stock is clear and light; boiling makes it cloudy. The béchamel is smooth, glossy and coats the back of a spoon.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Stock: 3 litres water reduced by evaporation to about 2 litres - about 1 litre lost over 2 hours. Béchamel: roux ratio fat : flour = 1 : 1 (50 g : 50 g) per 500 ml milk (100 g each per litre). Portions of 60 ml sauce: 500/60 = 8.3, so 8 portions.
precautions: Start stock in cold water to draw out flavour.
Simmer, never boil, stock.
Add liquid to roux gradually to avoid lumps.
Do not add salt to stock - it concentrates when reduced.
sourcesOfError: Rate of evaporation depends on heat and pot size.
commonMistakes: Boiling stock rapidly, making it cloudy and greasy.
Adding cold milk all at once to hot roux.
Colouring a roux meant to be white.
examTips: Know the ratio of bones to water and roux to liquid.
Name sauces made from each mother sauce (e.g. béchamel -> cheese/mornay sauce).

checkQuestions.q: Why should stock be simmered and not boiled?
options: To keep it clear and avoid a greasy, cloudy stock
checkQuestions.explanation: Boiling emulsifies fat and scum into the stock.

checkQuestions.explanation: Equal parts: 50 g each per 500 ml.

checkQuestions.q: 500 ml of sauce gives how many full 60 ml portions?

checkQuestions.explanation: Cold water draws out flavour and lets scum rise.

practicals.title: Roasting a whole chicken
practicals.topic: Study of food commodities and principles of cooking methods
practicals.aim: To prepare, truss and roast a whole chicken, calculate the cooking time and test for doneness.
safety: Wash hands and equipment after handling raw poultry; use a separate board.
Use oven gloves and lift trays away from the face.
Cook until the core temperature reaches at least 75 °C.
procedure: Weigh the chicken and calculate the cooking time.
Clean the bird, season inside and out, and truss to keep a neat shape.
Place on a bed of roots or a trivet, brush with oil and roast at 190 °C.
Baste every 15-20 minutes.
Test: juices from the thickest part of the thigh run clear, or the probe reads at least 75 °C.
Rest for 10-15 minutes, then carve and serve with roast gravy.
practicals.expectedObservations: The skin becomes golden-brown and crisp; the flesh is moist and the juices run clear. The bird loses weight as fat and water are cooked out.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Rule: 20 minutes per 450 g plus 20 minutes. Mass 1.8 kg = 1,800 g; 1,800/450 = 4; time = 4 x 20 + 20 = 100 minutes (1 hour 40 minutes). Cooking loss of 25%: cooked mass = 1.8 x 0.75 = 1.35 kg, enough for 4 portions (quarters).
precautions: Preheat the oven.
Baste to keep the meat moist.
Rest before carving so juices settle.
sourcesOfError: Oven temperatures vary; always test the core temperature.
commonMistakes: Undercooking poultry (pink juices).
Not resting, so juices run out on carving.
Using the same board for raw chicken and cooked food.
examTips: Explain the principle of roasting: cooking in dry heat with fat in an oven or on a spit.
Show cooking-time calculations step by step.

practicals.title: Grilling fish
practicals.topic: Study of food commodities and principles of cooking methods
practicals.aim: To prepare and grill whole fish (e.g. croaker or tilapia) using radiant heat and serve with suitable accompaniments.
materials: Onion rings and parsley/scent leaves for garnish
safety: Keep long sleeves and cloths away from the grill.
Handle charcoal safely; never use petrol to light it.
procedure: Scale, gut and wash the fish; make shallow diagonal cuts (score) on both sides.
Marinate with pepper, garlic, ginger, salt and oil for at least 20 minutes.
Preheat the grill and oil the bars to prevent sticking.
Grill for about 4-6 minutes each side, depending on thickness, brushing with oil.
Test: flesh is opaque and flakes easily at the bone.
Serve hot with lemon wedges, onion rings and a sauce or salad.
practicals.expectedObservations: The fish browns on the surface with grill marks, the scored flesh cooks through evenly and remains moist.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Marinade oil: 15 ml per fish x 4 fish = 60 ml. Total raw fish = 4 x 300 g = 1.2 kg. If cooking time is about 5 minutes per side, each fish takes about 10 minutes; grilling two at a time, four fish take about 20 minutes.
precautions: Score the fish so heat penetrates.
Turn only once to avoid breaking.
Oil the bars well.
sourcesOfError: Fish thickness varies; cooking time must be adjusted.
commonMistakes: Grilling at too low a heat, so the fish stews and sticks.
Turning repeatedly and breaking the fish.
examTips: Grilling is a fast, dry-heat method using radiant heat - state its advantages (quick, low fat).
Know suitable foods for grilling.

checkQuestions.explanation: Scoring lets heat reach the thick parts.

practicals.title: Baking: sausage rolls for a catering order
practicals.topic: Principles of cooking methods and practical demonstrations
practicals.aim: To bake a batch of sausage rolls using shortcrust pastry and cost them per piece for a catering order.
safety: Keep raw meat chilled until needed.
Use oven gloves; cool trays before handling.
procedure: Make shortcrust pastry by rubbing 250 g fat into 500 g flour and mixing with cold water; rest it.
Roll the pastry into long strips about 10 cm wide.
Roll the sausage meat into long sausages and lay them along the strips.
Dampen the edges, fold over, seal and cut into 24 equal rolls; brush with egg.
Bake at 200 °C for 20-25 minutes until golden and the meat is cooked.
Cool and cost the batch.
practicals.expectedObservations: Rolls are evenly sized, golden and flaky-crisp; the meat is fully cooked.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Costing (illustrative): flour N800, margarine N875, sausage meat N4,000, egg N200. Total = N5,875. Cost per roll = 5,875/24 = N244.79. Selling price at a 40% food cost = 244.79/0.40 = N611.98 (about N610-N615).
precautions: Cut all rolls the same size for portion control.
Seal well to prevent leaking.
Make sure the oven is fully preheated.
commonMistakes: Uneven rolls, giving inconsistent portions.
Underbaked pastry under the meat.
examTips: Explain the principle of baking: cooking by dry convected heat in an oven.
Give a full costing: ingredients, total cost, cost per portion, selling price.

Baking cooks food mainly by
checkQuestions.explanation: Baking uses dry convected heat in an oven.

checkQuestions.q: Why should sausage rolls be cut to equal sizes?
options: For portion control and uniform cooking
checkQuestions.explanation: Equal sizes give consistent portions and even cooking.

practicals.title: Laying table d'hôte and à la carte covers
practicals.topic: Types of food service and table laying/setting
practicals.aim: To lay a table d'hôte cover and an à la carte cover correctly and prepare a table for waiter/silver service.
apparatus: Cruet, ashtray-free table number, bud vase
safety: Carry glasses on a tray; hold by the stem.
Check for chipped crockery and glassware.
procedure: Lay the cloth with the centre crease running down the table and equal drop on each side.
Allow about 60 cm per cover.

Table d'hôte cover: lay all the cutlery for the set menu in order of use from the outside inwards (soup spoon, fish knife and fork, joint knife and fork, dessert spoon and fork), side plate and side knife on the left, wine/water glass above the joint knife.
À la carte cover: lay a fish plate or show plate, fish knife and fork, side plate, side knife, napkin and glass; further cutlery is laid course by course after ordering.
Add cruet, table number and bud vase; fold napkins neatly.
Inspect the table and polish any marks.
practicals.expectedObservations: Covers are evenly spaced and identical; cutlery is about 1-2 cm from the edge and aligned, giving a professional look.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: A rectangular table 180 cm long allows 180/60 = 3 covers on each long side, i.e. 6 covers in all (more if the ends are used).
precautions: Handle cutlery by the handles and plates by the edges.
Polish cutlery and glasses before laying.
commonMistakes: Laying an à la carte cover with all the cutlery for every course.
Placing the glass over the side plate.
examTips: Draw and label the covers when asked; know the difference between the two types.
Name the types of service: silver, waiter/plate, gueridon, buffet, banquet, self-service.

practicals.title: Dish costing and setting the selling price
practicals.aim: To calculate the cost per portion of a dish, set a selling price from a food-cost percentage and calculate gross profit.
materials: Ingredient list with prices (e.g. for egusi soup or jollof rice)
safety: Not applicable for a desk exercise; observe normal kitchen safety if the dish is also prepared.
procedure: Write the standard recipe with quantities for the stated number of portions.
Find the cost of each ingredient (quantity x unit price).
Add to find the total food cost and divide by the number of portions.
Set the selling price: selling price = cost per portion / food-cost percentage.
Calculate gross profit = selling price - food cost and express it as a percentage of selling price.
Record on a dish costing sheet.
practicals.expectedObservations: A standard costing sheet shows exactly how much each portion costs and ensures a consistent profit margin.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Total food cost for 4 portions = N2,400. Cost per portion = 2,400/4 = N600. With a 40% food cost: selling price = 600/0.40 = N1,500. Gross profit = 1,500 - 600 = N900 = 900/1,500 x 100 = 60% of the selling price.
precautions: Use current prices.
Include all items, even seasoning and oil.
Check arithmetic.
sourcesOfError: Prices change; costing sheets must be updated.
commonMistakes: Multiplying by the food-cost percentage instead of dividing.
Leaving out small ingredients.
examTips: Write the formula before substituting numbers.
Know the terms: food cost, gross profit, net profit, selling price.

practicals.title: Portion control and yield testing of meat
practicals.aim: To trim and cook a quantity of beef, measure the losses and calculate the number of portions and the true cost per portion.
safety: Use a sharp knife, cutting away from the body.
Keep raw meat chilled and separate from cooked food.
procedure: Weigh the beef as purchased and record the cost.
Trim fat, gristle and bone; weigh the trimmed meat.
Cook the meat and weigh the cooked yield.
Calculate the percentage losses and the number of 100 g cooked portions.
Calculate the true cost per portion.
Demonstrate portioning with scales and standard ladles/scoops.
practicals.expectedObservations: Meat loses weight both in trimming and in cooking (water and fat loss), so the number of portions is much less than the purchased mass suggests.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Purchased 5 kg at N6,000/kg = N30,000. Trimming loss 15%: 5 x 0.85 = 4.25 kg. Cooking loss 25%: 4.25 x 0.75 = 3.1875 kg cooked. Portions of 100 g = 3,187.5/100 = 31 full portions. True cost per portion = 30,000/31 = N967.74. Overall yield = 3.1875/5 x 100 = 63.75%.
precautions: Weigh accurately at each stage.
Use standard portion equipment.
sourcesOfError: Different cuts and cooking methods give different losses.
commonMistakes: Dividing the purchase cost by the raw mass portions (50) instead of the cooked portions.
Not allowing for trimming loss.
examTips: Show each loss step separately.
List aids to portion control: scales, scoops, ladles, portion-sized dishes, standard recipes.

checkQuestions.explanation: Standard ladles and scoops give equal portions.

practicals.title: Planning and writing a table d'hôte menu
practicals.aim: To plan and write a four-course table d'hôte menu for a function, in the correct sequence of courses, and calculate its price per head.
safety: Indicate allergens (e.g. groundnuts, shellfish) on the menu.
procedure: Note the occasion, number of guests, budget, season and any special dietary needs.
Choose dishes for each course following the classical sequence (e.g. hors d'oeuvre/starter, soup, main course with vegetables, sweet, coffee).
Balance colour, texture, flavour and cooking methods; avoid repeating main ingredients.
Write the menu neatly, centred, with correct spelling and consistent language.
Cost the menu and calculate the price per head.
Compare with an à la carte menu for the same restaurant.
practicals.expectedObservations: A good table d'hôte menu has a fixed number of courses at a set price, limited choice, and dishes that complement each other.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Food cost for 60 guests = N180,000, so food cost per head = 180,000/60 = N3,000. At a 40% food cost, price per head = 3,000/0.40 = N7,500.
precautions: Do not mix languages within a dish name.
Avoid repeating the same ingredient or colour in successive courses.
commonMistakes: Courses out of order.
Two heavy starchy courses together.
Misspelling dish names.
examTips: Know the meaning of table d'hôte, à la carte, carte du jour and plat du jour.
Present a neatly laid-out menu - layout carries marks.

practicals.title: Planning menus for vegetarians and for manual and sedentary workers
practicals.aim: To plan and prepare lunch menus to suit a vegetarian, a manual worker and a sedentary worker, using energy needs.
materials: Beans, moin-moin ingredients, vegetables, rice, yam, eggs, fish/meat (for non-vegetarians), fruits
safety: Keep vegetarian dishes and utensils separate from meat to avoid cross-contamination.
procedure: State the needs of each group: vegetarians need plant proteins combined (e.g. beans with rice/maize); manual workers need more energy; sedentary workers need less energy, more fibre.
Estimate the energy for the lunch as about one-third of the daily need.
Plan suitable menus (e.g. vegetarian: moin-moin, jollof rice, vegetable salad; manual worker: pounded yam, egusi soup with fish; sedentary: boiled yam with vegetable sauce and fruit).
Prepare one menu and present it attractively.
Justify the choices.
practicals.expectedObservations: The manual worker's meal is larger and more energy-dense; the sedentary worker's is lighter with more vegetables; the vegetarian meal combines legumes and cereals for good-quality protein.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Daily energy (illustrative): manual worker 3,300 kcal; sedentary worker 2,200 kcal. Lunch at one-third of the day: manual = 3,300/3 = 1,100 kcal; sedentary = 2,200/3 = 733 kcal (about 730 kcal).
precautions: Avoid animal products such as gelatine and lard in vegetarian dishes (and eggs and milk for vegans).
Use less oil for sedentary workers.
sourcesOfError: Energy needs vary with age, sex and body size.
commonMistakes: Giving vegetarians only starchy food.
Using meat stock in a vegetarian dish.
examTips: Give reasons linked to nutrients for each dish.
Define vulnerable groups (infants, pregnant and nursing mothers, the elderly, the sick).

checkQuestions.q: Which combination gives a vegetarian good-quality protein?
checkQuestions.explanation: Cereals and legumes complement each other's amino acids.

checkQuestions.explanation: Less physical activity means a lower energy requirement.

practicals.title: Preparing food and table accompaniments
practicals.aim: To identify suitable accompaniments for common dishes and prepare coleslaw and tartare sauce for service.
safety: Keep mayonnaise-based items chilled below 5 °C.
Use a guard on the mandolin.
procedure: List dishes and their accompaniments, e.g. fried fish - tartare sauce and lemon; roast beef - horseradish sauce and Yorkshire pudding; fried plantain - beans or eggs; suya - sliced onions and yaji pepper; soups - pounded yam, eba or fufu.
Coleslaw: finely shred cabbage and carrot, add a little onion, bind with mayonnaise and season.
Tartare sauce: chop gherkins, capers and parsley and mix into mayonnaise with lemon juice.
Lay table accompaniments: salt, pepper, sauces in sauce boats with underplates.
Chill and serve with the main dishes.
practicals.expectedObservations: Accompaniments add flavour, colour, texture and nutritive value, and correctly matched ones complement the main dish.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Coleslaw for 20 portions of 60 g = 20 x 60 = 1,200 g (1.2 kg). If the cabbage yield after trimming is 80%, purchase 1,200/0.8 = 1,500 g of vegetables.
precautions: Prepare cold sauces close to service and keep chilled.
Match accompaniments to dishes correctly.
commonMistakes: Serving the wrong accompaniment (e.g. mint sauce with fish).
Leaving mayonnaise salads at room temperature.
examTips: Distinguish food accompaniments (served with the dish) from table accompaniments (cruet, sauces on the table).
Learn the classic pairings.

practicals.title: Preparing and serving non-alcoholic drinks (chapman and fruit punch)
practicals.topic: Types of alcoholic and non-alcoholic drinks
practicals.aim: To identify bar equipment and prepare and serve non-alcoholic chapman and a fruit punch in batches.
materials: Angostura bitters (contains a little alcohol - omit for strictly non-alcoholic service)
safety: Use tongs or a scoop for ice, never glasses or hands.
Use clean, chipped-free glassware.
procedure: Identify bar equipment and glassware and state uses.
Chill all drinks and glasses.
Chapman (per glass): fill with ice, add orange and lemon/lime soft drinks in equal parts, a dash of blackcurrant cordial or grenadine, garnish with cucumber and orange slices.
Fruit punch batch: mix orange and pineapple juice with a little lime juice and soda water in a punch bowl, add sliced fruits and ice just before serving.
Serve from the right, holding glasses by the base.
practicals.expectedObservations: Drinks are cold, attractively garnished and correctly measured so each glass tastes the same.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Batch for 20 guests at 200 ml each = 20 x 200 = 4,000 ml (4 litres). If 1.5 litres of punch fills 7 glasses of 200 ml (1,400 ml) with 100 ml over, then 4 litres fills 4,000/200 = 20 glasses exactly.
precautions: Add ice and soda last to keep the drink cold and fizzy.
Measure ingredients for consistency.
commonMistakes: Scooping ice with a glass (it may break).
Garnishing carelessly.
examTips: Classify drinks: alcoholic (beer, wine, spirits, liqueurs) and non-alcoholic (juices, squashes, mineral waters, tea, coffee, cocoa).
Name items of bar equipment and their uses.

practicals.title: Identifying, using and maintaining catering equipment
practicals.topic: Care and maintenance of kitchen equipment
practicals.aim: To identify large and small catering equipment, and to clean and maintain a deep-fat fryer, a refrigerator and a mixer.
safety: Switch off and allow the fryer oil to cool completely before draining.
Unplug electrical equipment before cleaning.
Wear heat-resistant gloves.
procedure: Identify equipment (salamander, bain-marie, deep-fat fryer, bratt pan, food mixer, mincer, slicer) and state uses.
Fryer: switch off, cool, drain oil through a filter, wipe out sediment, clean with hot detergent water, rinse, dry fully and refill with filtered or fresh oil.
Refrigerator: remove food, switch off, defrost if necessary, wash with warm detergent water, rinse, sanitise, dry, switch on and reload once below 5 °C.
Mixer: unplug, remove attachments and wash them, wipe the body with a damp cloth.
Record refrigerator temperatures twice daily on a log sheet.
practicals.expectedObservations: Well-maintained equipment works efficiently, lasts longer and reduces the risk of fire and food poisoning.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Refrigerator log readings: 3, 4, 4, 6, 3 °C. Mean = 20/5 = 4 °C, within 1-5 °C, but the single 6 °C reading is above 5 °C and must be investigated (door left open, overloading or faulty seal). Freezer should be at -18 °C or below.
precautions: Never let water drip into hot oil.
Do not overload refrigerators - air must circulate.
Follow the manufacturer's instructions.
sourcesOfError: Readings taken just after opening the door are higher.
commonMistakes: Draining hot fryer oil.
Storing raw meat above cooked foods.
Using abrasives on stainless steel.
examTips: Identify equipment from diagrams and state one use and one maintenance point for each.
Know safe temperatures for fridges and freezers.

practicals.title: Cleaning and sanitising food-contact surfaces
practicals.aim: To carry out the stages of cleaning and sanitising a work surface and prepare a chlorine sanitiser of the correct strength.
safety: Wear gloves when handling bleach; never mix it with acids or other cleaners.
Label and date the diluted sanitiser.
procedure: Wash hands correctly and put on a clean apron and hat.
Pre-clean: remove loose food debris.
Main clean: wash the surface with hot detergent water.
Rinse with clean water.
Sanitise with chlorine solution (about 200 ppm) and leave for the required contact time.
Rinse (if required for food-contact surfaces) and air-dry or dry with paper towels.
Check hot food holding (at or above 63 °C) and cold holding (at or below 5 °C) with a probe.
practicals.expectedObservations: The surface is visibly clean and smells faintly of chlorine; correctly held food stays out of the danger zone (5-63 °C) where bacteria multiply rapidly.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: 5% bleach = 50,000 ppm available chlorine. To make about 200 ppm: dilution factor = 50,000/200 = 250, so about 4 ml bleach per litre of water (4 ml in 1,004 ml total gives 50,000 x 4/1,004 = 199 ppm).
precautions: Always clean before sanitising.
Use fresh sanitiser each shift.
Use colour-coded cloths for different areas.
sourcesOfError: Bleach loses strength with age and heat.
commonMistakes: Sanitising a greasy surface without washing first.
Using too strong a solution, which can taint food.
examTips: List the stages of cleaning in order: pre-clean, main clean, rinse, disinfect, final rinse, dry.

practicals.title: Fire safety and first aid in the catering kitchen
practicals.aim: To identify fire-fighting equipment, demonstrate the correct response to a fat fire, and apply first aid for burns and cuts.
apparatus: Fire extinguishers (water, foam, CO2, dry powder, wet chemical) or pictures
safety: Never attempt live fire demonstrations without a qualified supervisor; use a simulated drill.
Never use water on a fat or electrical fire.
procedure: Identify each extinguisher by its label colour and state the fires it can be used on.
Demonstrate the fire blanket on a (simulated) pan fire: turn off the heat if safe, pull the tapes, cover the pan completely, leave it covered for at least 30 minutes.
Demonstrate the PASS method: Pull the pin, Aim at the base of the fire, Squeeze the handle, Sweep from side to side.
Hold an evacuation drill and time it.
Practise first aid for burns (cool under running water for at least 20 minutes) and cuts (pressure, clean dressing).
Record accidents in an accident book.
practicals.expectedObservations: The fire blanket smothers a pan fire by cutting off oxygen. A well-practised team evacuates the kitchen quickly and in order.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Evacuation drill: 45 staff leave in 90 seconds. Rate = 45/1.5 minutes = 30 people per minute. If the target is 60 seconds, the team must improve to 45 people per minute.
precautions: Keep exits and extinguishers unobstructed.
Train all staff in the use of equipment.
Report all accidents.
sourcesOfError: Drills are calmer than real emergencies.
commonMistakes: Throwing water on burning oil, causing an explosive flare.
Removing the fire blanket too soon.
Moving a burning pan.
examTips: Match each extinguisher to the class of fire.
Give causes, prevention and first aid for common kitchen accidents.
